A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EduBench research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices support comparison, including matching material across substantial reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original model and human evaluations, evaluator-bias experiments, and results from distilling a Qwen2.5-7B model.

after.justification: V4 retains those empirical results and adds synthetic-query quality assessments and three-round human-evaluation results.

M1.justification: V4 adds a query-quality assessment component that selects a human-aligned evaluator and applies QwQ-32B to the full dataset (Section 2.4, Figure 3). The generation prompts, twelve response metrics, metric allocation and distillation strategies remain unchanged; no new filtering rule, architecture or training objective is reported.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same nine educational scenarios, Chinese and English coverage, subject categories and 18,821-item dataset. The dataset-count tables match. Query-quality auditing and repeated human ratings assess existing coverage rather than introduce new educational tasks or populations.

E2.justification: The original five response models and four response evaluators remain in their corresponding comparisons. V4 adds a query-quality evaluator comparison involving R1, GPT-4o and QwQ against human ratings (Table 6); Section 2.4 identifies the selected query evaluator as QwQ-32B.

E3.justification: V4 introduces an approximately 500-query audit using linguistic, content and task-specific criteria, MAE-based evaluator selection, and full-dataset scoring. Response evaluation changes from one human annotator to three. The stated distillation training size changes from 4,000 to approximately 17,000, although both appendix count tables list 17,983 training items; this establishes revised reporting, not that training was rerun.

E4.justification: Section 2.4 and Tables 1 and 6 add a substantial assessment of whether synthetic queries are linguistically sound, educationally appropriate and usable for their intended tasks. V1 lacks this direct dataset-quality analysis. The existing self-preference, reasoning-model preference and positional-bias experiments are retained unchanged.

E5.justification: V4 newly reports human evaluation over three rounds in Tables 17–18 and specifies three annotators, whereas v1 reports one annotator. It does not explain aggregation across rounds or add confidence intervals, dispersion estimates or human inter-rater agreement.

E6.justification: All matched, retained numerical tables are unchanged. V4 adds query-quality scores and three-round human results. In Table 17, the 7B model's metric average of 7.74 exceeds the 14B model's 7.69, whereas the original human ratings were 7.46 and 7.56 respectively. These are additional ratings under revised annotation conditions, not demonstrated model performance gains.

T1.justification: Neither version develops theoretical results or proofs. V1's generic score-averaging equation is omitted, but averaged scoring remains described; this removes explanatory formalization without changing mathematical reasoning. The added MAE serves as an empirical evaluation metric.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain the diverse educational benchmark, twelve-dimensional evaluation and competitive distilled 7B model. However, the introduction weakens the specific data-efficiency claim from achieving comparable performance with only 4,000 training examples to approximately 17,000.

C2.justification: V4 adds a rationale for synthetic data based on sparse or unstable real educational data and interprets the new query ratings as validating dataset quality. It removes v1's explicit single-annotator and synthetic-query realism limitations, while retaining the limitation that practical applicability has not been tested in real educational environments.

D1.justification: V4 supplies detailed query-quality scoring rubrics in Appendix D, but removes the abstract's code/data release statement and repository link without replacement. Existing generation prompts, training hyperparameters, GPU specifications and annotation-cost information remain.

R1.justification: Related-work coverage is substantially contracted and refocused: general benchmark discussions such as GLUE, MMLU and AlpacaEval and numerous application references are removed. Li et al. (2025), EducationQ and EduPersona are added, with more explicit positioning against examination-oriented, classroom-only and fixed-format evaluation.

P1.justification: Related Work moves from Section 2 to Section 6 and is extensively condensed and rewritten. The experimental subsection hierarchy changes, several explanatory passages are revised, and new query-evaluation appendices are integrated before the retained evaluation and prompt material. Author and contribution text also expands.

P2.justification: V4 adds Figure 3 and four tables, merges v1's metric-results and abbreviation tables into side-by-side subtables, and resizes the overview figures. Most appendix prose and prompt boxes change from single-column to two-column layouts, with substantial relocation and resizing of retained tables.

improvement.justification: V4 provides useful validation missing from v1 through direct query-quality assessments, explicit scoring rubrics and three-round human results. These make benchmark quality easier to assess. The gains remain limited: Table 6 does not report the stated MAE comparison, new human results are not reconciled with unchanged main tables, and the repository link and synthetic-data realism caveat disappear. The added evidence supports a modest net improvement.
